results.title: Metadata Driven ETL | Data Platform and Data Science
results.content: A data company just asked me if I’d like to participate as a panelist in a webinar about automating ETL pipelines in a few weeks time. If we have 100 source tables and 100 target tables, we will just be creating 100 pipelines (you can see how it’s done here using ADF .NET SDK). A better idea would be creating just one ETL pipeline, but this pipeline can read all 100 source tables and inserting them into 100 target tables (sequentially, one at a time). A metadata driven ETL means that the table name, column name, data type, etc. Then, based on those config tables the ETL/ELT pipelines read the source data, validate each column according to their data type and defined rules, and load the data to the correct target column. The main drawback is: that one pipeline needs to run in turns, processing each source table/file one by one. If your project is a data migration, and the data volume is not huge (say 10,000 rows x 100 tables) then in this case it is superb idea to use this metadata driven approach. Because data migration means that it is only for one-off, i.e. the ETL pipeline will only be run once, not every single day for many years. The entity level metadata stores the source and target table name, and their location/schema. The attribute/column level metadata stores the source and target column name, and their mapping + transformation, and their data types, plus validation rules such as not null, unique/PK and valid ranges (for numerical columns, e.g. must be a positive interger) and valid length (for text columns). If the source data is a relational database (RDBMS) or APIs, the population of the metadata/config tables can and should be automated. The column names and data types of the source tables can be extracted using information schema. In this day and age of data warehousing where we use cloud data platform like Snowflake and Databricks, a metadata driven ETL is a must. For the business users in each domain to do self-service on data creation, you will need to have metadata driven data loading. Metadata Driven ETL is required for Data Mesh.

results.title: How to Write Test Cases for ETL Pipelines: Complete Guide | Airbyte
results.content: ETL testing is essential to validate data completeness, correctness, consistency, performance, and security at every pipeline stage to prevent costly downstream failures. * Effective test cases define clear objectives, controlled test data, expected outputs, automated execution, and regression integration. ETL testing validates that data is correct, complete, and consistent at every pipeline stage. ETL testing ensures that data is correct, complete, and consistent at every pipeline stage**.** Unlike application testing that validates code logic, ETL testing validates data movement, transformation accuracy, and business rule enforcement. **Test for:** Calculation accuracy, null handling, data type conversions, and edge cases like leap years or timezone changes. A pipeline might be technically complete and correct but fail compliance testing if it doesn't mask customer data properly. Test how your pipeline processes missing data in required and optional fields. Application testing validates code logic, while ETL testing ensures that data is correct, complete, and consistent as it moves across systems. Every test case should define the input data, expected output, and validation rules.

results.title: GitHub - ndleah/AWS-ETL-pipeline: ⚙️ ETL pipeline on AWS using S3 and Redshift
results.content: A music streaming startup, Sparkify, has grown their user base and song database and want to move their processes and data onto the cloud. Their data resides in S3, in a directory of JSON logs on user activity on the app, as well as a directory with JSON metadata on the songs in their app. In this project, we will create an ETL pipeline to build a data warehouses hosted on Redshift. Each file is in JSON format and contains metadata about a song and the artist of that song. Log Dataset The second dataset consists of log files in JSON format generated by this event simulator based on the songs in the dataset above. To enable Sparkify to analyze their data effectively, they have implemented a Relational Database Schema, capable of being populated through an ETL pipeline. The fact table, specifically designed to store user song activities categorized as "NextSong," forms the foundation for the company's ability to relate and analyze users, songs, artists, and time dimensions. To populate the relational database, an ETL pipeline is employed, efficiently extracting the required information from both user behavior log files and corresponding master data of songs, subsequently transforming it into the schema. Fact Table \* \*\*`songplays`\*\* - records in event data associated with song plays i.e. records with page NextSong songplay\_id, start\_time, user\_id, level, song\_id, artist\_id, session\_id, location, user\_agent Dimension Tables \* \*\*`users`\*\* - users in the app \* \*\*`songs`\*\* - songs in music database \* \*\*`artists`\*\* - artists in music database \* \*\*`time`\*\* - timestamps of records in songplays broken down into specific units. In order to create ETL pipeline on AWS, The project includes four files:. * **main.py** is the main script that can run all modular scripts in this project (the whole ETL pipeline). * **create\_table.py** is where you'll create your fact and dimension tables for the star schema in Redshift. * **etl.py** is where you'll load data from S3 into staging tables on Redshift and then process that data into your analytics tables on Redshift. The `create_tables.py` and `etl.py` file can also be run independently as below:. s3-bucket redshift etl-pipeline data-modelling.
